title: The Bat Who Draws the Dark
creature: A bat who can describe a room she has never seen lit
summary: Joaquim is losing his sight, and the bat is the first thing in that house that does not talk around it.

chapters.title: The Word Nobody Uses
chapters.text: There was a word for what was happening to Joaquim and by the end of that spring he had heard every adult he knew avoid it. His mother said *your eyes*. The consultant in Porto said *the condition* and then, when pressed, said the actual name in a fast quiet way, once, and went back to *the condition*. His aunt said *this business*. His grandfather, who was in general the most reliable person in the house, said *what you've got*, which was somehow the worst of the lot because his grandfather did not otherwise talk like that about anything. The word is retinitis pigmentosa. It is not a difficult word. Joaquim had looked it up in the second week and had been reading about it steadily ever since, and he was thirteen and he knew a great deal more about it than most of the people carefully not saying it in front of him. What it means, in his case, is that the outside is going first. That is the part nobody outside the house ever gets right. People assume it is like a light going down. It is not. It is the edges: the field narrows, slowly, unevenly, over years, so that what he has is a good clear middle and a growing amount of nothing round it. He can read a page. He cannot see the person standing beside the page. By that spring he had walked into three door frames, a bollard, and, in front of most of his year, a fire extinguisher. The fire extinguisher is the one people always want to hear about and it was not the bad one. The bad one was a Tuesday in April when he put his hand out for a glass on the kitchen table and the glass was not where his hand went, and he knocked it, and his mother came across the room fast — genuinely fast, at a speed she had no reason to be capable of — and caught it before it went off the edge. Neither of them said anything. She put it back in the middle of the table, four centimetres from where it had been, and went back to what she was doing. Joaquim sat there and understood that she had been watching his hands for some time. And what he had noticed — what he had come to mind far more than the door frames — was that people had started arranging themselves. His mother put things away. His aunt moved chairs. At school there was a system, which nobody had discussed with him, whereby a boy called Rafa was always somehow on his left in a corridor. All of it was kind. All of it was done by people who loved him. And all of it happened in a silence so complete that Joaquim had begun to feel that the actual event — the thing occurring inside his own head — was a subject the entire world had agreed to handle by rearranging the furniture. He started going up to the attic in the evenings because it was the only room in the house nobody had prepared. His grandfather's house had a lot of rooms and every one of them had been quietly gone over. The rug in the hall had gone. The low table in the front room had gone. The chest on the landing had moved back against the wall in about February and nobody had ever remarked on it and Joaquim had walked past its new position four hundred times without once mentioning that he had noticed. The attic had a ladder and boxes and a water tank and no plan.

chapters.title: Something Working in the Dark
chapters.text: The attic at his grandfather's was reached by a ladder and had one bulb that had not worked since before Joaquim was born. He went up in the dark on purpose. That was the point of it. In the dark his condition was irrelevant, because in the dark nobody has any edges, and for an hour a night he was exactly as capable as anybody else in the world, which is to say not very. He sat with his back against a trunk and did nothing at all. It was the only hour of his day in which nothing was being managed. He would like that understood without it sounding like a complaint about his family, because it is not one. Every single thing they did was the right thing and he would have done the same. But there is a particular tiredness in being the object of continuous careful attention, and it does not go away by being grateful for the attention, and at thirteen he had no way at all of saying so. In the dark of that attic he was not the boy whose eyes were going. He was a person sitting in a dark room, which is a thing anybody can be, and it was restful in a way he has never quite got back. He heard her on the fourth or fifth evening. Not the flying — he had heard the flying from the first night and had assumed birds. What he heard on the fourth or fifth evening, when he had been sitting still long enough, was the other thing. It is a series of clicks and it is mostly too high for a person. What comes down into human range is the low edge of it: a fast dry ticking, right at the top of what an ear will take, that goes across the room and comes back. He could not hear all of it and he knows that now. What reaches a thirteen-year-old ear is the bottom of the range and there was a great deal going on above it, and one of the strange satisfactions of his twenties has been putting equipment on that attic and finding out how much he had been missing. At the time he had the low edge and it was enough. She was working. That is the word he arrived at and has never improved on. It was not flapping about. It was a search pattern — out along the ridge beam, down the gable, across, back — with the ticking speeding up whenever she came near anything and slowing when she was in open air. Joaquim sat in the pitch dark of that attic and listened to something map a room. It took perhaps forty seconds, which he timed on later evenings and which never varied by much. Out, down, across, back. Then a pause. Then again, and the second pass was faster than the first, because by then she was not mapping — she was checking what had changed. Nothing had changed. Nothing changes in an attic. She did it anyway, every night, for the whole of that spring and summer. He did not move for a long time, and when he finally did, the ticking came at him fast and hard and then stopped and went away, and he understood that he had just been drawn.

chapters.title: What She Knows About That Room
chapters.text: He read everything the library had, which was one book and a chapter in another, and then read online for six weeks, and this is what he found out. She sends a sound and the sound comes back and the time it takes tells her how far. That much everybody knows. What almost nobody knows is how much comes back with it. The pitch of the return tells her whether the thing is coming or going. The shape of the return tells her the texture — a curtain and a plank at the same distance sound completely different, and the difference is not subtle to her. Overlapping returns give her a moth's wingbeat frequency, which is how she can tell one insect from another in flight, in the dark, at four metres, in about the time it takes a person to blink. She does not build a fuzzy sense of the room. She builds a room. The bit that took him longest to accept was the resolution. He assumed, because everybody assumes it, that sound must be a coarse instrument — that she would be getting an approximate lumpy version of the world compared to the crisp one a person gets from eyes. That is not what the numbers say. At close range a bat can resolve a difference of well under a millimetre in the distance to a surface. She can find a wire in the dark that a person cannot see in daylight. There is no sense in which she is getting a rough draft. Joaquim sat with that for about a week and then got hold of the thing that mattered, and he got hold of it in the attic at nine at night with his back against a trunk. That bat has never seen the room. Not once. That attic has not had a working bulb since the 1990s and she is nocturnal and she has spent her entire life in and around a black space under a roof. There is no version of that room in her head made of light. There has never been one and there is not going to be one. And she knows it completely. Better than he does. She knows where every beam is and every nail and the loose board by the water tank and the exact position of the trunk he sits against, and she has never once bumped into any of it, and she is not managing or coping or compensating. She is not doing a worse version of seeing. She is doing a whole thing, all the way, that arrives at a room. He wrote that sentence in the back of an exercise book and looked at it for a while and then wrote underneath it, in smaller letters, the thing he had actually been trying to get at: *Nobody feels sorry for a bat.* Nobody stands in a doorway watching a bat's hands. Nobody moves a chest on a landing for a bat. Every book he had read described what she does with something close to awe, and not one of them had ever once described it as a way of getting by.

chapters.title: The Only One Who Said It
chapters.text: He tried to explain this to his mother in the kitchen and made a mess of it, because it came out as *there is a bat in the attic* and then as *no, listen*, and then as nothing, because she had gone pale at the bat and it took eleven minutes to get her off the subject of bats in the roof. He tried it on the consultant in Porto in July and got a smile. He got it out properly, in the end, to his grandfather, in the car, on the way back from Porto, because in a car you are side by side and nobody has to look at anybody. He said that everybody kept talking about what he was going to lose. He said that nobody had said a single sentence to him, in four months, about what he was going to have. His grandfather drove for about a kilometre. Then he said: "That's fair. That's a fair thing to say and I've been as bad as the rest." And then, after another while: "What is it that you'll have?" Which was, Joaquim thought at the time and still thinks, an enormous question to be asked by an adult, and the first one anybody had put to him that was not about appointments. He said he did not know yet. He said that there was an animal in the attic that had built a complete room out of nothing but sound and had never wanted a bulb, and that he was not saying he was going to be a bat, and that he was aware of how it sounded. His grandfather said: "Say it anyway." So Joaquim said that he had spent four months being handled by people who thought the important thing was the part going dark, and that he had started to think the important thing was going to be whatever he built instead, and that nobody could tell him anything about that because nobody in that house had ever had to build one. They were about six kilometres outside Amarante. His grandfather said, "Right," and put the indicator on, and pulled into a lay-by, and sat there for a bit with his hands on the wheel. Then he said: "Retinitis pigmentosa." "What?" "That's the name of it. I've not said it out loud since March and I've been ashamed of that for about a month." He put the car back in gear. "It's a rotten word and I'm not fond of it. But it's yours and you've had to carry it round on your own and that was not right of any of us." They did not talk for the rest of the way and it was a good silence. Joaquim is twenty-six. He has about eleven degrees of field left in the right eye and less in the left, and he works in acoustics, which everybody in his family finds either enormously moving or extremely funny depending on which of them you ask. The attic at his grandfather's has a working bulb now. It was done in 2019 by an electrician who was not told about anything. Joaquim goes up there when he visits, in the evening, and does not turn it on.
